messages.subject: Bayesian football model in rstan
parts:
Inspired by Andrew Gelman’s World cup model.I have been trying to translate the following football model by Baio and Blangiardo to stan. In the end I would like to reproduce Table 2 from the paper.


My model takes the following form (file "football.stan"):

data {
  int nteams;
  int ngames;
  vector[nteams] prior_score;
  int team_home[ngames];
  int team_away[ngames];
  int score_home[ngames];
  int score_away[ngames];
}

transformed data {
}

parameters {
  real home;
  real sig_att;
  real mu_att;
  real sig_def;
  real mu_def;
  vector[nteams - 1] att_free;
  vector[nteams - 1] def_free;
}

transformed parameters {
  vector[nteams] att;
  vector[nteams] def;
  vector[ngames] theta_home;
  vector[ngames] theta_away;

  # Constrain sum(att) = 0, sum(def) = 0
  # see: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1202
  for (k in 1:(nteams - 1)) {
    att[k] <- att_free[k];
    def[k] <- def_free[k];
  }
  att[nteams] <- -sum(att_free);
  def[nteams] <- -sum(def_free);

  for (i in 1:ngames) {
    theta_home[i] <- exp(home + att[team_home[i]] + def[team_away[i]]);
    theta_away[i] <- exp(att[team_away[i]] + def[team_home[i]]);    
  }
}

model {
# Priors
  home ~ normal(0, 0.0001);

  mu_att ~ normal(0, 0.0001);
  mu_def ~ normal(0, 0.0001);
  sig_att ~ gamma(0.1, 0.1);
  sig_def ~ gamma(0.1, 0.1);

  for (i in 1:(nteams - 1)) {
    att_free[i] ~ normal(0, sig_att);
    def_free[i] ~ normal(0, sig_def);
  }

  for (i in 1:ngames) {
    score_home[i] ~ poisson(theta_home[i]);
    score_away[i] ~ poisson(theta_away[i]);
  }
}



I run stan from within R using rstan

library("rstan");
d <- read.csv("seria_a_1991_1992.csv", header = TRUE);
d$score_home <- d[, 3]; 
d$score_away <- d[, 4];
d$idx_home <- d[, 5] + 1;
d$idx_away <- d[, 6] + 1;
teams <- as.character(sort(unique(d[, 1])));
nTeams <- length(teams);

data <- list(nteams = nTeams,
             ngames = nrow(d),
             prior_score = rep(1, nTeams),
             team_home = d$idx_home,
             team_away = d$idx_away,
             score_home = d$score_home,
             score_away = d$score_away);

stan_fit <- stan("football.stan",
data = data,
iter = 2000,
chains = 4);

plot(stan_fit, pars = c("home", 
                   "mu_att", "sig_att",
                   "mu_def", "sig_def",
                   "att[1]", "att[2]", "att[3]",
                   "att[4]", "att[5]", "att[6]"));



A look at the top 6 attack parameters att[1],…,att[6] seems to give a reasonable match with the first 6 entries from Table 2. What puzzles me is the fact that stan always seems to set parameters home, mu_att and mu_def to zero. I have used the same priors as in the paper.


Could somebody explain what is going on here, and why e.g. parameter home does not seem to have any affect in my stan model? I must be making some mistake in including the model parameters.


On a site note: Baio and Blangiardo refer to their choice of (hyper-)priors ~normal(0, 0.0001) as "flat priors”. Could somebody explain why this would be considered a flat prior? Surely normal(0, 0.0001) is not really flat?


Thanks,

Maurits


PS. I am attaching the full model with data and R script.

parts:
Stan uses the scale (std dev) parameterization of
normal, like R, so this is probably not what you
meant:

home ~ normal(0, 0.0001);

Those diffuse gamma priors can also be problematic; we
usually recommend half-Cauchy or even half-normal.

Also, you can vectorize to make this all much much
faster and the code much simpler. This:

for (i in 1:ngames) {
theta_home[i] <- exp(home + att[team_home[i]] + def[team_away[i]]);
theta_away[i] <- exp(att[team_away[i]] + def[team_home[i]]);
}

for (i in 1:ngames) {
score_home[i] ~ poisson(theta_home[i]);
score_away[i] ~ poisson(theta_away[i]);
}
can be replaced with:
for (i in 1:ngames) {

log_theta_home[i] <- home + att[team_home[i]] + def[team_away[i]];
log_theta_away[i] <- att[team_away[i]] + def[team_home[i]];
}

score_home ~ poisson_log(log_theta_home);
score_away ~ poisson_log(log_theta_away);

The poisson_log function takes its parameter on the log scale.

With our new array slicing and indexing, both of these can
be replaced with the two-liner:

score_home ~ poisson_log(home + att[team_home] + def[team_away]);
score_away ~ poisson_log(att[team_away] + def[team_home]);

This isn't even in the manual yet --- I need to update it
ASAP with examples!

- Bob

Dear Bob.

Thanks for the fast reply and for pointing out the issue with the normal prior. Indeed Baio and Blangiardo parameterise their normal priors in terms of mean and precision (1/sigma^2). I should've read their paper more carefully and picked that up.

Upon changing the priors for home, mu_att and mu_def in stan to
normal(0, 1e5)
I get a non-zero estimate for home. That also eliminates my previous question about flat priors. All good!

Stan-derived estimates for mu_att and mu_def are not informative, for example mean(mu_att) +- sd(mu_att) = 696 +- 99762.
I was expecting stan to drive mu_att and mu_def to zero due to shrinkage. Could somebody point out why this is not the case?

Also, thanks Bob for tidying up my stan model code; I was aware of certain vectorisations; others are new to me ("array slicing and indexing"). I usually leave for-loops in my stan models to help with (initial) readability and debugging.

One more question about the vectorisation and code optimisation: Let's say I would like to store estimates for parameters theta_home and theta_away; would it be faster to do what you did (i.e. use the poisson_log) and then inverse-transform the log_theta's back to the linear scale in a separate generated quantities block? Or use poisson and theta_home, theta_away parameters in the transformed parameters block like in my original example?

And a last one:

Those diffuse gamma priors can also be problematic; we 
usually recommend half-Cauchy or even half-normal.

Would you mind elaborating? Problematic in what way?


Thanks,
Maurits

 for (i in 1:ngames) {

parts: Because you center the parameters:

att[nteams] <- -sum(att_free);
def[nteams] <- -sum(def_free);
the intercept can't get absorbed into the parameters here:

for (i in 1:ngames) {
theta_home[i] <- exp(home + att[team_home[i]] + def[team_away[i]]);
theta_away[i] <- exp(att[team_away[i]] + def[team_home[i]]);
}

For theta_home, the parameter home will act as an intercept. If you
really wanted an intercept, it'd look like this:

log_theta_home[i] <- alpha + home + att[team_home[i]] + def[team_away[i]]);
log_theta_away[i] <- alpha + att[team_away[i]] + def[team_home[i]]);

Then alpha is the intercept either way (it may need to be negative on one
side to make sense --- you'll have to check), and home is an additional offset
for away games.

That's basically like setting up def as centered and att as being centered
around alpha (or vice-versa).

- Bob
